required_tuples.rationale: POST /login with a wrong password is denied with 401 and no token material, however often it is repeated.
POST /login with a wrong password is denied with 401 and no token material, however often it is repeated.
POST /login with a malformed JSON body is rejected with 400 and no token material or refresh cookie.
POST /login with a missing or null username or password key is rejected with 400 and no token material.
POST /login with empty username or password strings reaches authentication and is denied with 401 and no token material.
A browser login returns the fixture user with an access token, refreshToken:null and a bookmarks array, and sets an HttpOnly refresh cookie that is Secure exactly when the request is HTTPS.
A browser login returns the fixture user with an access token, refreshToken:null and a bookmarks array, and sets an HttpOnly refresh cookie that is Secure exactly when the request is HTTPS.
A login answer carries the user projection, the default library id, the server settings without secrets, an ereader device list and the server source, and the cookie lifetime is the 30 day default.
POST /login matches the username case-insensitively and the answer carries the stored username.
POST /login with X-Return-Tokens: true returns the refresh token in user.refreshToken, sets no refresh cookie, and stores exactly that token in a new sessions row of the user.
POST /login with X-Return-Tokens other than the text true behaves as a browser login: refreshToken null and a refresh cookie.
POST /login with an unknown username is denied with 401 and no token material.
A denied or rejected login creates no sessions row and sets no refresh cookie.
A user who was deactivated is denied at POST /login with 401 and no new session, and can log in again once reactivated.
After an admin changes a user's password, POST /login with the old password is denied with 401 and the new password logs in.
A non-root user stored without a password hash (as OpenID-created users are) is denied at POST /login with 401 for any password, including the empty one, and gets no session.
When the active auth methods no longer include local, POST /login is refused with an error status and no token material; enabling local again restores it.
With RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_MAX=3 the fourth POST /login in the window is answered 429 with an error message, even with valid credentials, and no session is created.
A root created without a password logs in only with an empty password; any non-empty password is denied with 401.

POST /auth/refresh with the refresh cookie answers a new access token and refreshToken null, sets a rotated HttpOnly refresh cookie with the request-security and 30 day lifetime, and moves the old token to lastRefreshToken in the one sessions row.
POST /auth/refresh with x-refresh-token answers user.refreshToken equal to the rotated token stored in the sessions row, and the refresh cookie carries the same token.
When both the x-refresh-token header and the refresh cookie are sent, the header token's session is rotated, the cookie's session is untouched and the refresh token is returned in the body.
Replaying a just-rotated refresh token inside the grace period answers 200 with a fresh access token and the already rotated refresh token, without rotating the session again.
After two rotations the first refresh token matches neither refreshToken nor lastRefreshToken and is denied with 401, while the previous one still replays inside the grace period.
With REFRESH_TOKEN_GRACE_PERIOD=2 a rotated token is denied with 401 once the grace period is over, while the current token still refreshes.
POST /auth/refresh with neither cookie nor header is denied with 401 and an error message.
POST /auth/refresh with garbage, a wrongly signed refresh token, or an access token is denied with 401 and an error message.
A denied refresh changes no sessions row.
A refresh token of a deactivated user is denied with 401 and leaves the sessions row unchanged; after reactivation the same token refreshes.
A refresh token whose sessions row has expired in the database is denied with 401 and the row is removed, although the token itself is still valid.
With REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRY=2 a refresh token past its lifetime is denied with 401 and its sessions row is removed.

POST /logout with the refresh cookie answers 200 {redirect_url:null}, expires the refresh_token and auth_method cookies, deletes that sessions row and keeps the user, so the token no longer refreshes.
POST /logout with the x-refresh-token header deletes that sessions row and answers redirect_url null.
POST /logout needs no authentication and without any refresh token answers 200 {redirect_url:null} and changes no sessions row.
Repeating POST /logout with an already revoked refresh token answers 200 {redirect_url:null} again and changes nothing else.
POST /logout with an unknown or malformed refresh token answers 200 {redirect_url:null} and deletes no sessions row, also with allDevices=1.
Logging out one session deletes only that sessions row; another session of the same user still refreshes.

With OpenID configured with an end-session URL, POST /logout carrying auth_method=openid and an openid_id_token cookie answers that URL with id_token_hint and the same-origin post_logout_redirect_uri (none for openid-mobile), expires the auth_method and openid_id_token cookies and deletes the session.
POST /logout?allDevices=1 deletes every sessions row of the token's user and no row of other users.
POST /logout?allDevices=1 with a just-rotated (grace) refresh token still deletes all sessions of its user.
POST /logout with allDevices=true (not 1) deletes only the presented session.

POST /init on an uninitialised server answers 200 and persists one active root user with the given username, a bcrypt password hash, a token and the full root permission set, and that user can log in.
Before POST /init /status reports isInit false with the config and metadata paths and login is denied; afterwards it reports isInit true without paths.
POST /init with an empty newRoot creates the root user named root with an empty password hash.
A second POST /init is denied with 500, creates no user and leaves the first root's credentials working.
POST /init on an installation that already has a root user is denied with 500 and neither adds a user nor changes the existing ones.

POST /api/authorize with a valid bearer token answers the login payload of that user (user, userDefaultLibraryId, serverSettings without secrets, ereaderDevices, Source) and creates no session or cookie.
Repeating POST /api/authorize answers the same user and default library and adds no sessions row.
userDefaultLibraryId follows the user's library permissions: the first accessible library, and again the first library once all libraries are allowed.
POST /api/authorize also accepts the access token as ?token= query parameter and the legacy non-expiring user.token as bearer, both authorizing the same user.
An active API key used as bearer token authorizes as the key's user.
With JWT_SECRET_KEY set, tokens signed with that secret authorize the user they name, tokens signed with another secret are denied, and the secret is not stored in the server settings.
POST /api/authorize without a token, with garbage, with a wrongly signed access token or with a refresh token as bearer is denied with 401.
Denied authorize requests change no sessions row and set no cookie.
Access tokens and API keys of a deactivated user are denied with 401 and work again after reactivation.
An inactive API key is denied with 401; activating it through PATCH /api/api-keys/:id authorizes it and deactivating it denies it again.
An API key created with expiresIn 2 authorizes at first, is denied with 401 once expired, and its row is then deactivated.
With ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRY=2 an access token authorizes at first and is denied with 401 once expired; a refresh yields a working token.

A native client logs in with X-Return-Tokens, uses the access token, refreshes with x-refresh-token, uses the new access token and logs out, after which the refresh token is dead and the session row is gone.
A browser logs in, refreshes twice with the rotating refresh cookie, and logs out with the latest cookie, after which neither the latest nor the earlier cookie refreshes.
Parallel refreshes with one refresh token all succeed and return one and the same rotated refresh token, which is the token stored in the session row.
When the access token has expired the API answers 401 and a refresh with the still valid refresh token yields a working access token.
PATCH /api/me/password with the current refresh token answers new tokens, revokes the user's other sessions and the old refresh token, and keeps the current session on the new tokens.
PATCH /api/me/password without a refresh token answers 200 and deletes every session of the user; the new password logs in and the old one does not.
PATCH /api/me/password with an x-refresh-token that matches no session answers 200 and deletes every session of the user.
PATCH /api/me/password with a wrong current password answers 400 and leaves the password and every session unchanged.
When an admin sets another user's password through PATCH /api/users/:id all that user's sessions are deleted while the admin's own sessions stay.

With the default configuration the access token is a JWT (userId, username, type access, exp one hour after iat), the refresh token has type refresh and expires after 30 days, sessions.expiresAt is about 30 days away after login and rotation, and rotation sets lastRefreshTokenExpiresAt about 10 minutes ahead.
With the default grace period a rotated token still refreshes right after rotation, and is denied once the stored grace timestamp has passed, while the current token keeps working.

Collection PATCH and POST need update, DELETE of a collection needs delete: an update-only user is denied DELETE (403, row kept) but may patch and remove a book (bookId removal is exempt from delete), a delete-only user is denied PATCH and POST (403) but may delete.
The playlist item add/remove and batch add/remove routes answer 403 to another user (admin included) and leave the playlist's items unchanged, while the owner may use them.
GET /api/playlists lists only the caller's playlists, and POST /api/playlists/collection/:id creates a playlist owned by the caller that no other user lists.
A deactivated user's token is denied with 401 on playlist, progress and listening-session routes, creates nothing, and works again after reactivation.

Progress and listening sessions are per user: each user's lists contain exactly their own rows, a progress write leaves other users' rows untouched, and another user's sessions are visible to admins only.

POST /api/users keeps the requested permission flags, library allowlist and tag selection, persists them inside the permissions column and answers them split into permissions, librariesAccessible and itemTagsSelected.
Creating a user emits user_added with the new user to admin sockets and not to an ordinary user's socket.
A permission update through PATCH /api/users/:id persists, answers the user and emits user_updated to the acting admin's sockets only, not to the updated user or other users.
An ordinary user is denied with 403 on the user administration and API key routes and nothing is created, changed or deleted.
The same denials hold for another ordinary user and when the requests are repeated.
A playlist can be read, updated and deleted only by its owner: another user, even an admin, gets 403 and the playlist is unchanged; an unknown id is 404.
The owner renames and deletes their playlist, the row follows, and playlist_removed goes to the owner's socket only.
A user without update and delete permission can read a collection but POST, PATCH and DELETE collection routes answer 403 and change nothing.
A user with update permission can create a collection; after an admin revokes update the same token is denied with 403 and no collection is added.
A user limited to the podcast library gets 403 for items and the item list of the other library, 404 for its collections, and sees only the podcast library in the library list.

A user restricted to a selected tag reaches only items with that tag (403 otherwise, and only those in the item list); with selectedTagsNotAccessible the selection is inverted and untagged items stay visible.
A user with accessAllTags false and no selected tags gets 403 for every item it requests directly.
An item marked explicit is denied with 403 and hidden from the list for a user without explicit-content access and visible for one with it; unmarking makes it visible again.

An item hidden by a tag rule or by the explicit-content rule is missing from the library search, personalized shelves, series list and author counts of that user while the admin still sees it, and a user without library access gets 403 on all of them.
Changing a user's tag selection through PATCH /api/users/:id takes effect for their existing access token.
A user who may update but cannot access the item's library gets 403 for PATCH /api/items/:id/media and the item's tags and updatedAt are unchanged.
An admin who is not root gets 403 for PATCH and DELETE of the root user and the row is unchanged.
Repeating the root-user PATCH and DELETE as non-root admin keeps answering 403 and never alters the root's sessions or row.
User list and user detail show the root user's legacy token as an empty string to an admin and in full to root.
DELETE /api/users/:id of the caller's own id answers 400 for admin and root and deletes nothing.
Missing credentials, an invalid type, a taken username, protected keys, non-object permissions and unknown users are rejected with 400 or 404 and change no user row.
POST /api/users ignores non-boolean permission values, unknown permission keys and non-string library lists, keeps the type defaults, and creates the user inactive when isActive is omitted.
A non-root admin creates and deletes an ordinary user: the row appears and disappears, user_added and user_removed go to admin sockets only, and the deleted user's token is denied.
After deactivation a user's login, access token, API key and refresh token are all denied with 401, and all work again after reactivation.

Ordinary users get 403 on API key routes; admins get 400 for a missing name, bad expiresIn, missing or unknown user and a non-boolean isActive, and 404 for unknown keys; none of this changes the apiKeys table.

An admin may create keys for ordinary users (row records user and creator) but gets 403 creating a key for root or changing a root-owned key; root may do both; deleting a key removes the row and its token stops working.
